claims.text: The starting catalyst is a nanoscale Pt-based or Pt-rich catalyst with uniform particle size and composition optimized for ethanol oxidation.
A small fraction of a secondary non-PGM metal will be introduced to form a surface or near-surface Pt alloy while particle size and morphology are held unchanged.
The proposed mechanism applies to electrochemical ethanol oxidation under alkaline, moderate-potential fuel-cell-like conditions.
Alloying Pt with the secondary non-PGM metal shifts the d-band center of Pt active sites.
Introducing a secondary metal can perturb the local electronic structure of a multimetallic catalyst.
The shifted Pt d-band center produces more moderate adsorption energies for ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Ethoxy, acetaldehyde, OH, and poisoning species are key adsorbed intermediates or species whose binding governs the proposed behavior.
Electronic modulation promotes sequential electron and proton transfer and inhibits catalyst poisoning.
The relevant ethanol-oxidation pathway involves transfer of 12 electrons and 12 protons.
The modified catalyst will have a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than the unmodified Pt catalyst.
The modified catalyst will have a higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the unmodified Pt catalyst.
The modified catalyst will favor complete oxidation of ethanol to CO2 over partial-oxidation products.
The modified catalyst will exhibit greater durability than the unmodified Pt catalyst.
The proposed electronic mechanism may cease to apply at extreme pH, very high overpotentials, or when mass transport dominates.
The magnitude of the effect depends on the identity and concentration of the secondary metal and on synthesis-dependent alloy structure.
The hypothesis is declared falsified if alloy addition produces neither statistically significant performance improvements nor a suitable d-band shift.
